doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

title: Being in the moment while improvising
summary: The mind is fast; getting out of your own way, listening instead of judging, time moves through people.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: People — the phrase “in the moment” shows up a lot. I think you’ve said it, playing jazz in the moment. And I’ve thought about it and I wonder if you think that there’s so much going on when you’re improvising because you’re in the moment but you’re also remembering or trying to remember what you just played, shall I play it again, how many choruses do I have, like wow, the brain must be very hyper intensive during improvisation.

Well I don’t think we’re aware of how fast our mind works. It’s really, really fast. Like when you have a thought and then you have another thought and then you have another thought. They could be all over the place but they just pop up, pop up, pop up. And it’s like that when you play and it’s really, you’ll hear the expression you have to “get out of your own way.” But that’s a good description of what it means to be in the moment, to get out of your own way, to — if you’re going to be in the flow of time, if you’re going to be in the stream, then you don’t, even though you have to be aware of the context of where you are and what you’re playing, whether it’s chord changes, whatever, whether it’s physically where you are on the stage. Even though you are aware of all that you can’t really be judging it. You don’t have time to — well as I said before — it’s how you recover from what you perceive as a mistake. If you dwell on something and you know, the world will pass you by. The tune will certainly pass you by. If you — well as Jon

Hendricks said, he watched his hand write the lyrics, you watch yourself play the solo. You hear yourself in the real time that everybody else hears you. And the extent to which you can do that, just listen to what you’re playing rather than judge what you’re playing or try to play something, you’ll be in the moment. And it’ll feel better even though, as I said before, you can’t hear yourself while you’re doing something. You’re not a good judge of what you sound like ever. The process still has a very physical quality to it so that you know when you’re getting out of your own way. You know when you’re not stopping the flow of time. I have a funny expression which is people don’t move through time, time moves through people. Time is not something that’s just consistent and out there and we’re walking around and everybody experiences the same time. Time is a function of how we feel. And we feel very differently every moment. So when we’re playing, when we’re improvising, particularly this would apply to a fast tempo. The way to play a fast tempo is to let go. If you try to hang on real tight you can’t play that. But if you let go you can just flow with the tempo. So there’s something in there about what it means to be in the moment. It’s hard to talk about it.
